name: Sunscreen daily habit
lead: Daily sunscreen use is the practice of applying a broad-spectrum sun protection product to the face every day, typically as part of a skincare routine, with the aim of preventing sunburn, redness, uneven tone and signs of photoaging.[1]

It is among the better-supported practices in appearance culture. Wikipedia reports that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, and cites studies in which daily use was associated with smoother, more resilient skin.[1] A dermatology trial also found daily SPF 15 use protected against UV-induced histologic damage.[2]

paras: SPF measures how much sunburn-producing UVB reaches the skin; SPF 15 lets through about one-fifteenth under standard test conditions. Higher SPF does not extend duration, and reapplication about every two hours is advised. Broad-spectrum products also cover UVA.[1]
Wikipedia says guidelines recommend SPF 30 or higher and that most people apply only a fraction of the tested amount, reducing protection.[1]

A 2000 study compared daily with intermittent sunscreen application and examined effects on UV-induced skin damage in humans, using SPF 15 applied daily.[2] Wikipedia also cites a 2013 Australian study of about 900 people in which daily broad-spectrum use over 4.5 years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin, and a small study reporting reversal of photoaging signs in 12 weeks with daily SPF 30.[1]

A 2019 study of a tinted SPF 30 moisturizer reported improved barrier measures and appearance in rosacea-prone skin, and a 2026 study reported pediatric safety testing of a mineral SPF 40 within a skincare regimen.[3][4] Those studies were of specific products.

Wikipedia reports that some ingredients can cause allergic contact dermatitis, that sunscreen can reduce vitamin D synthesis though deficiency is rare with typical use, that benzene contamination was found in some aerosol products, and that some filters harm coral and are banned in places such as Hawaii.[1] It says public health bodies generally judge skin cancer risk to outweigh unproven concerns about approved filters.[1]

timeline.event: Greiter introduces the sun protection factor (SPF).[1]

card.summary: Daily SPF on the face; backed by dermatology guidance and studies on skin damage and photoaging.
card.note: Allergic reactions to some filters are reported; most people under-apply.

quick.overview:
Applying broad-spectrum sunscreen to the face every day is a staple of skincare routines, aimed at preventing redness, dullness and photoaging.

Trials and reviews cited by reference sources link daily use to less UV skin damage and smoother skin, and sunscreen is reported to help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
quick.mechanism: Sunscreen filters absorb or reflect ultraviolet light. SPF rates UVB protection; broad-spectrum products also cover UVA.
quick.risks: Some ingredients can cause allergic contact dermatitis; vitamin D synthesis can be reduced though deficiency is rare. Regulation varies: OTC drug in the US, cosmetic in the EU.
